title: Pennsylvania Railroad S1 locomotive at the 1939 World’s Fair
lede: Raymond Loewy’s shroud for the longest steam locomotive ever built: a bullet nose with a round headlamp and speed lines that run the whole length of engine and tender.
summary: A dark bullet-nosed steam locomotive with parallel speed lines along its length. Raymond Loewy for the Pennsylvania Railroad, 1939.

creator.name: Raymond Loewy (shroud); Pennsylvania Railroad, Altoona Works (builder)

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected two Gottscho-Schleisner photographs of No. 6100 at the New York World’s Fair: [PRR S1.jpg](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PRR_S1.jpg) (Library of Congress reproduction number LC-G613-35557, dated 15 July 1939) and [gsc.5a18640](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:World%27s_Fair,_railroad_exhibit_locomotives._LOC_gsc.5a18640.jpg), both at 1920 px on Commons. The stored image is the first.

styles.note: Loewy’s best-known streamline design: a bullet nose, a round headlamp, and groups of parallel speed lines along a very long horizontal body.

context: Built at the Pennsylvania Railroad’s Altoona Works and completed on 31 January 1939; Raymond Loewy designed the streamlined shell. At 140 ft 2½ in with tender it was the longest reciprocating steam locomotive ever. At the 1939 New York World’s Fair it ran on a roller platform at 60 mph under the lettering “American Railroads”, part of a combined 27-railroad exhibit. It served from 1939 to 1946 and was scrapped in 1949. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad_class_S1).
observed: The locomotive is very long and low; the photograph is more than twice as wide as it is tall and still crops the tender.
The front is a rounded bullet nose with a large round headlamp in a ring at its center.
Groups of two and three thin bright lines run from the nose back along the whole engine; the tender carries the same parallel lines and the words “AMERICAN RAILROADS” in spaced capitals.
The shell is a smooth, dark, glossy surface; small star-shaped badges are the only other marks.
A railing encloses the exhibit, and the fair’s disc-shaped canopy and a lighting mast appear at right.
interpretation: The S1 is the rubric’s speed line in its purest form: a few parallel lines drawn along a long dark body, meeting at a round headlamp. It also shows that the style works on a dark ground, not only on cream.
borrow: Start a group of parallel lines at a circular element and run them to the far edge of the layout.
Space the capitals of a long label widely so it reads as a band.

images.alt: Black-and-white photograph of a very long streamlined steam locomotive behind a railing: a rounded bullet nose with a round headlamp, thin parallel lines along the whole body and tender, and the words American Railroads on the tender.
images.caption: PRR S1 No. 6100 at the New York World’s Fair, 15 July 1939. Gottscho-Schleisner, Inc., Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, LC-G613-35557, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PRR_S1.jpg).

rights.statement: Commons marks the Gottscho-Schleisner photograph public domain; the Library of Congress lists no known restrictions on that collection. A locomotive is a useful article, not protected by copyright in the United States, its country of origin. Raymond Loewy died in 1986; the shroud’s shape is not a separable artwork.
